Although it may shorten labour without increas- ing maternal or neonatal harm, it has not been shown to reduce the rate of caesarean section.3 Various techniques are available for induction of labour, and the choice may be influenced by the ripeness of the cervix and whether the membranes are intact or have rup- tured. Mechanical methods are commonly used and may be all that is needed to induce labour. UK guidelines sug- gest that sweeping of the membranes (manually separating the lower membrane portion from the uterine wall during vaginal examination) should be offered to women at term. It increases the likelihood of spontaneous labour within 48 hours and birth within one week, and reduces the frequen- cy of formal induction of labour.4 However, it may cause maternal discomfort, irregular contractions, and bleeding.5 Laminaria tents or hygroscopic cervical dilators may be used to stimulate cervical ripening.1 Amniotomy (deliber- ate rupture of the membranes and release of amniotic fluid) may also be used to stimulate labour, once the cervix be- comes favourable.2 When pharmacological induction of labour is required, a prostaglandin or oxytocin is generally used. UK guidelines4 suggest that, regardless of cervical status, prostaglandins are preferred to oxytocin in all wom- en with intact membranes, but either may be used in wom- en who have ruptured membranes as neither method then offers any particular advantage. However, others1,2,6 sug- gest that a ripened cervix improves the chance of success- ful labour induction, and WHO7 recommends oxytocin alone if the cervix is favourable but that a prostaglandin or a mechanical method (Foley catheter) should be used to ripen an unfavourable cervix before induction. As prostaglandins can both ripen the cervix and initiate uterine activity, they induce labour that is similar to spon- taneous labour.1 Overall, compared with oxytocin, pros- taglandins seem to improve the rate of successful vaginal delivery, lower the rate of caesarean section, reduce the need for epidural analgesia, and be associated with im- proved maternal satisfaction.4 The intravenous and oral routes have been associated with frequent adverse, partic- ularly gastrointestinal, effects8,9 and intravaginal dosage is now preferred. The intracervical route is no more effective than the intravaginal route, and is no longer recommend- ed.4 Dinoprostone (prostaglandin E2) is the most widely used prostaglandin and has been given by various routes.
